questions.title: How did the D.C. Circuit have appellate jurisdiction over this FOIA summary judgment?
questions.question_body: The panel affirms a district court's grant of summary judgment to the FBI on a FOIA request. I'm assuming jurisdiction came from 28 U.S.C. § 1291 as a final decision, but does anything about the use of sealed, ex parte declarations or the ongoing-update requirement affect appellate jurisdiction? Is there any FOIA-specific appellate jurisdiction wrinkle I should be aware of, or is this just a straightforward final-judgment appeal?

questions.title: What establishes Article III standing for a FOIA requester here, and why didn’t the court discuss it?
questions.question_body: The opinion doesn’t mention standing, yet FOIA plaintiffs still need injury-in-fact, traceability, and redressability. Is denial of access to records alone sufficient Article III injury for FOIA (so courts often don’t discuss it)? Does the fact that the records concern national security or an ongoing investigation change the standing analysis at all?

questions.title: How can the court review de novo but still defer to the FBI under Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: The panel says FOIA summary-judgment rulings are reviewed de novo, but also that the FBI’s decision to invoke Exemption 7 is entitled to deference, especially in national-security contexts (citing Campbell and CNSS). What exactly is reviewed de novo versus what receives deference? Is the deference about the weight accorded to agency affidavits (presumption of good faith), while legal conclusions remain de novo?

questions.title: Why do ongoing criminal investigations qualify as 'enforcement proceedings' under 7(A)?
questions.question_body: Exemption 7(A) protects records if disclosure could reasonably be expected to interfere with 'enforcement proceedings.' The court, citing CREW and Juarez, treats an ongoing criminal investigation as such a proceeding. From a statutory-interpretation standpoint, how did courts get from 'proceedings' (which sounds formal) to including pre-charge investigations, and what limits exist on that reading?

questions.title: Did the court miscite § 552(b)(7)(B) when discussing 7(A), and does that affect the analysis?
questions.question_body: In Part IV.B the opinion quotes the 'could reasonably be expected to interfere' language but cites § 552(b)(7)(B) instead of 7(A). Is that just a scrivener’s error? If so, does it have any substantive consequence, considering 7(B) deals with fair trial rights rather than interference with enforcement proceedings?

questions.title: What made the Hardy and Bender declarations sufficiently specific despite CREW’s warning about vague assertions?
questions.question_body: CREW says vague claims that an investigation is 'ongoing' can be insufficient for 7(A). Here, the court acknowledges Bender’s public declaration was 'surprisingly terse,' but deems it adequate in light of the earlier Hardy declarations (including ex parte detail) and the district court’s prior 'seemingly' satisfied finding. Do courts accept a short 'update' affidavit if earlier public and sealed submissions provided the specificity? What level of public specificity is required post-CREW?

questions.title: When are FOIA affidavits considered 'stale,' and what triggers a duty to update them?
questions.question_body: The district court denied summary judgment without prejudice because the initial declarations might have become stale over time and ordered an update. Are there established benchmarks or factors for when staleness requires updated declarations (e.g., elapsed time, changed circumstances, nature of the investigation)? Or is this a case-by-case, discretionary call?

questions.title: How did the FBI satisfy the 'compiled for law enforcement purposes' requirement under Pratt/Campbell here?
questions.question_body: The court requires a rational nexus to a law-enforcement duty and a connection to a security risk or violation of federal law. Publicly, Hardy said the records related to national security/terrorism investigations and ties to persons involved in such violations; the ex parte declaration added detail. Is that combination (general public assertions plus sealed specifics) typically enough to meet Pratt’s nexus test? Does the use of the file in immigration proceedings affect the 'law enforcement purposes' analysis?

questions.title: Do immigration removal proceedings count as 'enforcement proceedings' for 7(A), or was the court relying only on criminal investigations?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly frames the relevant 'proceedings' as ongoing criminal investigations (citing Juarez). But Farahi’s file was used in immigration removal litigation. Can civil administrative proceedings like removal independently satisfy 7(A)? If so, why did the court emphasize criminal investigations instead of DHS removal proceedings?

questions.title: Was it appropriate for the court to rely on allegations from an Eleventh Circuit immigration decision to support an 'ongoing' investigation?
questions.question_body: Because it couldn’t disclose sealed details, the panel cited public allegations about Farahi (e.g., ties to Al Qaeda figures) from an Eleventh Circuit opinion. Are courts permitted to use such allegations as contextual support for the plausibility that an investigation is ongoing? Do those allegations have to be proven facts, or is their existence in the public record enough to bolster the inference?

questions.title: What is required to justify categorical withholdings under 7(A), and how did Farahi forfeit his challenge?
questions.question_body: The opinion says that when an agency withholds by category, the categories must be 'sufficiently distinct' (citing Gallant and CREW), but concludes Farahi forfeited any challenge for not explaining why the FBI’s categories were overbroad. What does an adequate challenge to categories look like in practice (e.g., specific Vaughn-index critiques)? How specific must the agency’s category descriptions be to allow meaningful adversarial testing?

questions.title: How demanding is the segregability obligation when sensitive information is interspersed throughout, and was ex parte proof alone enough?
questions.question_body: The district court found, based on Bender’s supplemental ex parte submission, that no reasonably segregable non-exempt material remained, citing Mead’s 'interspersed line-by-line' principle. In 7(A) cases, do courts require in camera review of samples or the records themselves, or can detailed affidavits suffice? What counts as 'reasonable steps' to segregate under § 552(a)(8)(A)(ii) in an investigation file of 10,000+ pages?

questions.title: Do sealed, ex parte declarations in FOIA raise due process concerns, and how are they reconciled with FOIA’s in camera review provision?
questions.question_body: The court notes ex parte submissions 'handicap FOIA plaintiffs' but are sometimes necessary to avoid disclosing the very information at issue (citing Perioperative). Are there constitutional constraints (e.g., due process) on relying heavily on ex parte declarations? How does § 552(a)(4)(B)’s in camera review authority interact with or limit the use of ex parte affidavits?

questions.title: Why didn’t the court reach other exemptions (like 7(C), 7(D), or 7(E)) once 7(A) applied?
questions.question_body: Given the nature of the records (counterterrorism files), other 7-series exemptions might have applied. Is it standard practice for courts to stop at 7(A) if it fully resolves the case? If the agency asserted multiple exemptions below, must the court address them, or can it affirm solely on 7(A)?

questions.title: What evidence must the government provide to show disclosure 'could reasonably be expected to interfere' beyond generic 'tipping off' rationales?
questions.question_body: The court accepts the FBI’s explanation that release would tip off targets to the scope of the investigation, a common 7(A) rationale (citing CNSS). When, if ever, do courts require more document-specific or category-specific showings of interference? How does CREW’s skepticism toward boilerplate assertions play into the required level of detail?

questions.title: What is the role of in camera inspection of the records versus reliance on agency affidavits in Exemption 7(A) cases?
questions.question_body: The opinion relies on agency declarations (some ex parte) and doesn’t mention the district court conducting in camera review of the actual records. Under § 552(a)(4)(B), when is in camera inspection expected or required, particularly for segregability or to test 'ongoing investigation' claims? Do courts avoid in camera inspection in 7(A) cases as a matter of practice?

questions.title: How does the court reconcile FOIA’s pro-disclosure presumption with strong deference in national-security contexts?
questions.question_body: FOIA is generally pro-disclosure, but the panel emphasizes deference to the executive on national security and counterterrorism investigations (citing CNSS). Is there a doctrinal framework explaining how the pro-disclosure presumption operates where national-security justifications are invoked under 7(A)? Does the burden meaningfully shift in practice, or does 'deference' just affect how much detail is demanded in the affidavits?

questions.title: If the investigation ended during the appeal, would that moot the 7(A) justification, and what happens then?
questions.question_body: Exemption 7(A) depends on pending or reasonably anticipated proceedings. If those ended while the case was on appeal, would the exemption evaporate? Would the proper remedy be a remand for reprocessing with updated declarations, or could the court consider post-judgment facts to affirm/deny?

questions.title: Did Farahi waive challenges to the use of ex parte submissions by not objecting below?
questions.question_body: The panel notes Farahi did not oppose the district court’s acceptance of ex parte declarations and says he therefore can’t challenge the court’s reliance on them. Is failure to object treated as waiver/forfeiture in FOIA cases? Are there any exceptions (e.g., plain error or structural concerns) that would allow a later challenge to ex parte reliance?

questions.title: Can a FOIA plaintiff obtain discovery to test the agency’s declarations in a 7(A) case like this?
questions.question_body: Given the heavy reliance on agency affidavits (some sealed), is civil discovery available to challenge the FBI’s assertions about pending proceedings or segregability? What is the standard for allowing discovery in FOIA cases (e.g., a showing of bad faith or contradictory evidence), and how does the national-security context affect that?
